text: Administrative Services.  OVERVIEW.  THERE are four major issues of relevance to the Administrative Services portfolio:  Commercialisation, reform of purchasing, public works and support for the Government's environment and social justice objectives. Commercialisation of most of the Department of Administrative Services' businesses has been underway since 1987. The Government's commercialisation reform initiatives have led to clearly measurable improvements in productivity, profitability and customer focus. Overall the Commonwealth has benefited—as a user, through greatly improved service quality and tower prices; and as an owner, through improvements in business performance and returns on investment. The Coalition has questioned whether DAS should be in competition with the private sector and has raised related issues such as alleged unfair advantages and competitive neutrality. A commercialised DAS has had a net positive effect on the efficiency of what were previously monopolistic, highly regulated markets— around SI billion in actual or potential Government business has been opened up to the private sector. The Federal Labor Government has completely overhauled the Commonwealth's procurement processes and policies to maximise opportunities for Australian and New Zealand industry development and to improve the administration and accountability of purchasing within government—all without compromising quality or price. As a result of the Government's policies, significant progress is being made in opening up access to government markets by small and medium enterprises (SMEs), implementing electronic commerce and promoting the capability of local industry. As part of the Federal Labor Government's major reforms to the construction industry, it has created the Public Works Policy Group (PWPG) to ensure that the Commonwealth, as a key client of the industry, implements the reforms to the same extent as the private sector. The Department plays an important role in helping the Government meet its national and international environmental responsibilities and its social justice objectives. It has encouraged the use of environmentally preferred paper products and energy rated appliances through its purchasing and has refused to deal with companies in breach of Affirmative Action legislation Many DAS businesses give practical support to the government's objectives through their commercial activities—most notably, through the Halon Bank, a collection and storage facility for halon gas which is a severe depleter of the ozone layer.  ABORIGINAL FLAG.  The Coalition's Position.  “Any attempt to give the flags official status under the Flags Act would rightly be seen by many in the community not as an act of reconciliation but as a divisive gesture ... Such a move would be quite inappropriate ... No matter how these flags bulk large in the affections of our indigenous people, they can only ever be symbols for one section of the Australian community" (John Howard, media release "Playing Politics with Flags " 4/7/95)  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government decided on 20 June 1995 that the flags of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples would be proclaimed as official flags. The proclamation of the flags was undertaken following recommendations in two reports; Recognition, Rights and Reform prepared by the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission, and the report of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation Going Forward: Social Justice /or the First Australians.  Comment.  - The Liberal Party is represented on the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation.  - Mr Patrick Dodson. Chair of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, along with many indigenous groups, supported the Government's move.  - A Herald-McNair Poll showed that a large majority of Australians supported the Government's decision to grant official recognition to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags. The nation-wide poll (conducted 12-14/7/95) showed that a total of 66% of voters approved (42% supported and 24% strongly supported). Total opposition was limited to 26% (with 14% opposed and 12% strongly opposed).  PURCHASING REFORMS.  The Coalition's Position.  The Shadow Minister for Industry, Commerce and Public Administration, the Hon. John Moore MP, has stated (Canberra Times report 4/12/95) that he intends to 'get rid of the two-envelope tendering system' because he believes it distorts the marketplace.  LABOR'S POSITION.  In the 1994 White Paper on Employment and Growth the Federal Labor Government announced a series of measures to maximise the industry development outcomes for ANZ suppliers. The measures are designed to ensure agencies undertake a more rigorous examination of potential Industry development outcomes in their purchasing decisions. They include the Endorsed Supplier Arrangement; the establishment of the ISONET (Industrial Suppliers Office Network) Board and enhancement of ISO resources; and the implementation of the Industry Impact Statement/Two Envelope Tendering requirements. The two-envelope tendering system applies to acquisitions over S 10m. Tenderers are required to include a second envelope with their bid which outlines the tenderer's Industry development proposal. The second envelope focuses both the bidden' and the buyers' attention on the wider Implications of their bid.  Comment.  The Department of Industry, Science and Technology has concluded that, since its implementation in April 1995, the Endorsed Supplier Arrangement (an IT supplier pre-qualification scheme) has directly resulted in $866m additional investment in the Australian IT industry over the next four years. About 100 companies have already been endorsed under the scheme. ISONET Ltd was launched in June 1995. It helps Commonwealth agencies identify competitive ANZ suppliers of goods and services. The Industry Impact Statement/ Two Envelope Tendering system requires agencies to consider industry development issues in evaluation of tenders for acquisitions over $10m. Proposals are currently being evaluated for 5 major projects (Oct 95 figure).  Arts. OVERVIEW.  THE MAJOR issues in the arts are ensuring an ongoing commitment to extend access to the arts and cultural heritage, recognising that most Australians appreciate the arts through mass media, responding to challenges of rapid developments in communications technology and globalisation by Ac development of Australian content in traditional forms and multimedia, copyright reform are indigenous cultural issues. The Federal Labor Government has recognised the far reaching importance of the arts to Australia and has put in place a comprehensive cultural policy, Creative Nation. The Coalition has responded with general commitments. It claims that "..the Coalition has a long, proud tradition of support for the Arts ... " (J Howard, Politics and Patriotism, 13 December 1995). This is an attempt to deny the hostility to the arts contained in Fightback! and other earlier policies. In Fightback!, the Coalition wanted to cut our premier cultural institution, the ABC, by $50 million a year, to restructure and cut the Australia Council and made thinly veiled threats towards many other cultural institutions.  Extension of access: The Prime Minister reflected the importance of the Arts to the Government by declaring arts as a Cabinet position and creating a new portfolio 6f Communications and the Arts to reflect the growing synergies between the broadcasting and telecommunications sectors and the arts. The Federal Labor Government has provided over $1 billion in direct support for the arts (including the ABC and SBS) this financial year. In Creative Nation, the Commonwealth's first ever cultural policy statement provided a strong policy base for arts development and S270 million for new programs especially in multimedia and music and over $11 million in regional touring.  Changes In communications technology: The Federal Labor Government has responded to challenges facing the cultural industries through rapid developments in communications technology and increasing globalisation by providing Government investment in multimedia. Reflecting the emerging multimedia industry internationally. Government support for multimedia production has been provided through an $84 million dollar integrated package of support. In contrast, the Coalition has attacked these initiatives as "money down the drain".  Mas Media: Ongoing support for the Film and television production industries has been increased to over $150 million each year with new film and television production funds and initiatives including an $11 million SBS Independent and a $60m Commercial TV Production Fund. Australian content roles for TV have been extended including requiring a minimum of 55% Australian content. A code also applies to radio broadcasts. In the past, the Coalition has consistently attacked funding for bodies like the Film Finance Corporation and the Australian Film Commission. Now, while they "commit" to retaining these important organisations, they pointedly do not commit to a specific level of support.  Copyright reform: Copyright has been singled out for major reform including a decision to introduce an electronic transmission right, settling a moral rights regime and in-principle support for extended performers rights. The Government has also confirmed the parallel import rules. A new copyright law reform body has been established to ensure that the copyright law protects copyright in the new communications environment. The Opposition has responded with only general statements.  Indigenous Issues: The Federal Labor Government has funded the Gallery of Aboriginal Australia and the National Institute for Indigenous Performing Arts Training. The Government established the Return of Indigenous Cultural Property and the Indigenous Cultural Heritage Protection Programs to protect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander heritage.  ARTS. FUNDING OF FILM, TELEVISION & MULTIMEDIA PRODUCTION.  The Coalition's Position.  "A Coalition Government will maintain the existing three-tiered structure comprising direct subsidies to film-makers, incentives for private investors and Australian content requirements", Howard—Screen Producers Association, 9 November 1995.  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government provides annual funding of S1SO million for production through film fundings and production agencies such as the Film Finance Corporation, Australian Film Commission and Film Australia). Its funding of the national broadcasters (ABC and SBS) also assists in funding production of Australian material. The Government also maintains, and has recently strengthened, Australian content requirements for TV. Minimum Australian content on TV has been increased to 55% and the number of hours of children's drama is being doubled. Through training Institutions such as the National Film, Television and Radio School the Federal Labor Government also supports the development of skills and talents used in Australian productions.  Comment.  The Opposition has not stated the level of support it would provide Their commitment is, therefore, hollow. The record of the Coalition in supporting film funding is poor. Previously the Coalition has proposed the abolition of the AFC and indicated that they would disband plans for the FFC (June 1987). The Coalition has continually failed to specify the level of support for production funding—support which it has specified for the ABC and SBS  ARTS. PARALLEL IMPORTATION OF SOUND RECORDINGS.  The Coalition's Position.  "Microeconomic reform has either stalled or is going backwards in the areas which are the direct responsibility of the Commonwealth Government. The record is sad but clear. The back-flip on the 1992 decision to remove restrictions on parallel imports on compact discs", Howard—"The Role of Government" 6 June 1995.  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government has established and funded Ausmusic ($l.2m a year) to provide support In the development of Australian Contemporary Music. Through Ausmusic's Midas scheme the Federal Labor Government is providing $500,000 for development of artists and repertoire and touring. Through Playing Australia the Federal Labor Government provides assistance to tour contemporary bands. The Federal Labor Government announced a $270m Investment package for the music Industry in April 1995. The expansion of the Triple J network provides a national network with a major focus on developing new Australian acts. Under the Federal Labor Government's broadcasting regime, rock/pop radio stations must play at least 25% Australian music. As part of its support for the development of Australian content, the Federal Labor Government supports retaining parallel Import restrictions hi cultural Industries to support. In particular Australia's music industry.  Comment.  Howard's comments are evidence that the Coalition's newly found support of the cultural industries and copyright is lip service. The truth is to be found in the negative policies in Fightback. The copyright boundaries provided by parallel import restrictions are essential to protecting our cultural industries such as contemporary music  Arts. COPYRIGHT REFORMS.  The Coalition's Position.  "The Coalition recognises that the need to provide fair and adequate protection of economic and morel rights is a first order issue for the arts community. If elected to government, we will treat the establishment of an up-to-date and workable copyright regime as the single most urgent reform in the arts portfolio". Howard, Screen Producers Association, 9 November 1995.  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government:  - Will introduce a world first electronic transmission right and is drafting legislation for Introduction In the next session of Parliament.  - Is drafting legislation on moral rights for Introduction in the next session of Parliament.  - Has given in principal support for the extension of performers' rights.  Comment.  Coalition pays only lip service to copyright and does not detail its proposals.  The only major copyright policy expressed is to remove parallel importation rules contrary to maintaining a viable Australian copyright market and support for moral rights.  ARTS. NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AUSTRALIA  The Coalition's Position.  The Coalition will support the construction of a National Museum at Yarramundi", Howard, ABC Radio, Dec 1994.  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government has funded the first stage of the National Museum on Acton. This is the Gallery of Aboriginal Australia. It has announced stage two, a $12m program to make Old Parliament Home Into a Social and Constitutional History Museum. A design competition for stage three, an environment museum at Yarramundi, has been announced. Federal Labor's commitment la to deliver an Innovative Museum to all Australia. It will be based in Canberra but not necessarily on a single site. There is a network of museum presences across the country, from the Old Parliament House and the Gallery of Aboriginal Australia in Canberra to Sydney Customs House and to new sites or gateways in other States. It will also be an interactive Museum which is available at a click of a computer at their local library, school or community centre. It will develop and deliver on-line material on our cultural heritage through the "Australia's Story—Our National Collections On-line Program.  Comment.  The Coalition will create an institution which Australians are likely to visit only once or twice in their lives. Labor is building a national museum for all Australians which is accessible throughout (lie country. The Coalition's proposal is an example of Senator lan MacDonald's proposition to shadow Cabinet that they make regional infrastructure promises because they can (to paraphrase) promise the world in this area without actually having to deliver anything.  Arts. NATIONAL CULTURAL NETWORK.  The Coalition's Position.  "We will establish a National Cultural Network which will enable our heritage and cultural collections to lie more accessible, especially in rural and regional Australia", Howard, Politics and Patriotism", 13 Dec 1995.  LABOR'S POSITION.  "Australia's Story: Our National Collections On-Line" launched on 6 December 1995 In Innovation Statement. It provides $10 million to digitise cultural material and make it available through all schools and libraries. Additional funding is to be provided to the National Museum of Australia to increase the rate of Its digitisation program to enable more Australians to access on-line material on their cultural heritage.  Comment.  The coalition provides no details on the "National Cultural Network" whereas Labor has been implementing a program for our National Cultural Initiatives to digitalise cultural material and make it available through Government resourced terminals in libraries and community centres.  ARTS. ACCESS FOR REGIONAL AND RURAL AREAS.  The Coalition's Position.  "A Coalition Government will put renewed emphasis on providing opportunities for our artists to demonstrate their talents by touring in Australia and overseas", Alston, Cultural Frontier. 6 October 1994.  LABOR'S POSITION.  Creative Nation promised another $11.7 million over 4 years to take the arts across Australia including through a new Festivals Australia program to give access to arts to regional and rural areas. 1995 brought $l million In funding to 61 projects through Festivals. Playing Australia and Visions of Australia programs have expended $14 million in funding over the last 3 years—over 400 different projects have been made possible.  Comment.  The Government has shown its commitment to the arts in regional and rural areas through nearly $20 million spending in the last 3 years.  The Opposition has only empty promises.    ABORIGINAL AND TORRES STRAIT ISLANDER AFFAIRS. OVERVIEW.   If EVER there was a policy-free zone in the Coalition it is in the area of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs. After Alexander Downing's blundering foray into Coalition policy on land rights in the deserts of the Northern Territory in 1994, on which he was accompanied by the current shadow minister, it was announced that the entire policy would be reviewed. More than 18 months have passed and there's still no sign of a result What we do know about the Coalition is firstly, that it is opposed to reform and social justice for Australia's indigenous peoples, as demonstrated in the Parliament when it voted against the Government's ground-breaking native title legislation, and secondly, that if "Fight Back" is anything to go by, the Coalition is likely to significantly slash the portfolio's budget, impacting on the poorest and most disadvantaged Australians. Set against this negativity and policy vacuum, stand the Government's proud achievements in responding to the High Court's historic decision in Mabo with its native title and land fund legislation, and its support for the continuing development of the indigenous social justice initiative. The primary portfolio issues for the Government, in addition to these major policy beachheads, are as follows:  - maintaining the pressure on State and Territory governments to implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody.  - improving Commonwealth/State financial relationships to obtain greater efficiency and accountability in the delivery of housing and infrastructure programs to Aboriginal communities.  - reviewing cultural heritage protection legislation—including seeking to provide effective copyright protection in the area of intellectual property.  - monitoring the effectiveness of and developing necessary amendments to the ATSIC Act, and reviewing (lie legislation relating to Aboriginal councils and associations.  There is much still to be achieved in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs policy and the Government is committed to continuing the process of change and social justice.  The Coalition's complete absence of policy in this area is a damning indictment and a demonstration of their utter cynicism and deceit which more than anything shows why they should and will remain in opposition.  Attorney-General's Portfolio. OVERVIEW.  THE Coalition has provided no detail of its alternative policies for this portfolio to date because, as Senator Vanstone has put it, the Government might "pinch them". They have criticised Government policy for not going far enough, but there have been no pronouncements about the changes the Opposition would make to improve the legal system should they gain office. The Prime Minister launched a major legal policy statement on 18 May 1995 with many initiatives across a very wide range of areas. The Justice Statement describes significant improvements which will be made to the legal system, including: reducing crime, protecting consumers, reinforcing human rights, simplifying legislation and making it more accessible to all Australians, improving legal aid services and making the resolution of disputes outside the legal system a practical alternative to legal proceedings.  Family services have been funded to expand pre-marriage relationships courses, marriage and family skills training and financial counselling for families. The Government has given the Family Law Act and its operations a comprehensive overview to make it clear that the interests of children come first. The "Safer Australia" campaign has as its strategy a national approach to reduce crime and build safer communities. Additional funding will be provided for legal aid and community legal centres so that more people can gain easier access to the legal system. At least one specialist women's legal centre will be established to serve the needs of women in every State and Territory.  Attorney-General's. RACIAL HATRED.  The Coalition's Position.  "We do not support civil remedies for racial harassment, but support criminal prohibitions along the lines of the vilification offences contained in the NSW legislation, with minor changes. We want community education as a key factor in controlling racial discrimination/vilification/ violence, and would introduce a $10 million package to support this " (Amanda Vanstone, Media Release, 7 March 19%).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government has enacted civil remedies. It remains convinced of the need for criminal sanctions to deal with extreme racist behaviour and has committed itself the introduction of another bill to include men protection in the Crimes Act In the next Parliament. The Government has committed $2.S2 million over 3 years to HREOC to allow it to administer me civil complaints scheme. Including for an information/promotion program.  Comment.  The Coalition's proposed criminal offence of serious racial vilification does not cover acts of inciting racial hatred as proposed by the Government. The Coalition hence would not deal with the precursors of violence as the Government would.  In omitting a civil sanction, the Coalition fails to provide an avenue for victims of racial harassment, abuse or intimidation to personally seek redress.  Attorney-General's. FAMILY SERVICES.  The Coalition's Position.  "We will introduce programs to reverse the (rend of increasing levels of family breakdowns." (Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995 and John Howard, Fair Australia speech to ACOSS, October 1995). "We will ensure that young Australians are given more opportunities to be better prepared for raising children." (Litres; Party Speakers Notes, November 1995, and John Howard, Fair Australia Speech to ACOSS, October 1995). "We will increase the resources available for marriage education and family counselling." {Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government provides substantial funding for family services. This funding was increased In the Justice Statement. The Federal Government has increased by 50% funding for family skills training which aims to promote positive parenting and non-violent problem solving targeting disadvantaged families.  Funding has been doubled.  Grants for relationship counselling In 94-95 totalled $20.671m.  Extra funding has been provided for community development officers to improve access for non-English speaking people to access the family services programs  Comment.  The Government has acted, through the Justice Statement, to reinforce its ongoing commitment to families with a range of initiatives to help families avoid legal problems and deal with difficulties and disputes.  Attorney-General's. FAMILY SERVICES.  The Coalition's Position.  "We will deliver counselling and other services at a local community level as far as possible." (Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995). "We will deliver a new homeless youth pilot program " (John Howard's Fair Australia Speech to ACOSS. October 1985).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Government's Justice Statement emphasised and has committed considerably increased funding to community based family services, including In regional and rural areas. Adolescent mediation and family therapy programs were set up in response to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission report on youth homelessness. Funding of $l.5m has been provided in 1995-6. Justice Statement Increased funding for this program by 55% to enable the expansion of services to rural and regional areas.  Comment.  The Coalition's proposal includes a requirement to attend mediation to attempt reconciliation with family. Service providers with extensive practical experience widely consider this kind of coercive approach destructive.  Attorney-General's. COURTS & TRIBUNALS.  The Coalition's Position.  TELEVISING COURT APPEARANCES.  "We would not allow unrestricted access to the courts by the electronic media, so that they could pick bits and pieces and excerpts and highlights." (Amanda Vanstone on ABC Radio 2CN— Elizabeth Jackson, 6 October 1895).  COMPOSITION OF JUDICIARY. "The Government has failed to make more female appointments to both the Federal Court and the Family Court "(Amanda Vanstone on Radio SAA, 13 May 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Government has serious reservations about televising court appearances. It believes the risks that the presence of cameras will influence the presentation of evidence in criminal cases are too great while there is no place for cameras in Family Court matters. There may be tome value in allowing cameras in the High Court or Federal Court in civil matters to Improve understanding of the legal system. The Federal Labor Government believes the Judiciary should reflect community values. Whilst merit must be the over-riding factor in Judicial appointments, the Government is actively working to widen the pool of talent qualified for the bench to include women, people of non-English speaking background and people of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander descent.  Comment.  There were brief experiments by State Courts with televising court appearances in 1995, notably in Victoria in the Supreme Court and the Magistrates Court, but they have generally been greeted with scepticism by the Australian public. A US-style system following such trials as the OJ Simpson case, have made Australians wary of such experimentation. The Federal Labor Government has a very good record of appointing female Judges. Over the past three years it has appointed 4 female judges out of a total of 8 appointments to the Family Court and 4 female judges out of a total of 17 appointments to the Federal Court. These appointments are far in advance of the numbers appointed by the Coalition during its term of office.  Attorney-General's. BUSINESS LAW.  The Coalition's Position.  "Will cut the red tape, the regulation and the paperwork that bedevil so many hard-working small business operators and deter so many potential new ones "  (John Howard 'The Australia I Believe In', 15 December 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  When the Second Corporations Law Simplification Bill passes in 1996 most small businesses will be operating almost entirely under a new, easy-to-follow, companies system. Labor has already massively cut red tape for all Australian companies, including no longer requiring companies to lodge accounts, cutting the need for a company to keep five registers and no longer requiring annual general meetings for proprietary companies. It will be much easier to start and run a company. Companies can now have a single member and a single director. Labor has substantially strengthened Investor protection. The Australian Securities Commission is proving an effective corporate watchdog. A new disclosure regime ensures an informed market. The next Parliament will see a new right of statutory derivative action allowing shareholders to take legal action on behalf of a company against its officers or others, as well as a new and more certain legal regime for the collective investments industry.  Comment.  Instead of mouthing rhetoric, Federal Labor has put in the hard work to strip away an array of unnecessary or redundant requirements in the Corporations Law. The small business Guide is a new easy-to-use guide for small business to assist small business in understanding the new less-burdensome Corporations Law.  Attorney-General's. NATIVE TITLE.  The Coalition's Position.  "We will retain the Native Title Act but reserve the right to amend it to ensure its effective operation." (John Howard "The Australia I Believe In', 15 December 1995)  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Native Title Act:  • provides a practical means for dealing with native title without constant litigation.  • ensures the validity of past grants, such as mining titles.  • enables future grants to be made validly, even If claims for native title have been made or determined.  • provides for a co-operative approach between levels of government, recognising that the States and Territories have primary responsibility for land management.  • encourages mediation and negotiation, but If this talk, it provides specially adapted tribunal and court procedures for native title issues.  Comment.  The Government accepts that the Act may need amendment to improve its operation, but the Opposition's track record of resisting the recognition of the reality of native title suggests that any changes the Opposition would make would be at the expense of indigenous peoples' interests.  Attorney-General's. THE REPUBLIC AND THE CONSTITUTION.  The Coalition's Position.  PEOPLE'S CONVENTION.  • "We will ensure proper community involvement in the review of Australia's Constitution, including our form of government, by holding a People's Convention in 1997." (John Howard 'The Australia I Believe In'. 15 December 1995).  • "If a consensus emerges from the People's Convention regarding the Head of State, that consensus will be promoted by the Government at a constitutional referendum. If no consensus emerges, then the Australian people will be asked to vote on a series of options for changes to establish which of them they desire." (John Howard, 'The Australia I Believe In'. 15 December 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The basic outline of the Federal Labor Government's position on the republic is as follows:  • Establishment of an Australian Head of State ('the President') appointed by a two thirds majority of the Commonwealth Parliament to:  — perform ceremonial and representational duties.  — exercise powers currently exercised by the Governor-General on the advice of the Federal Executive Council.  • Removal of all references in the Constitution to Ac Queen, the Crown and the Governor-General.  • Retention of "Commonwealth of Australia" as the title of an Australian republic.  • Retention of membership of the Commonwealth of Nations.  • Freedom to the States to decide their own constitutional arrangements.  Comment.  In April 1993 the Federal Labor Government established the Republic Advisory Committee to prepare an options paper which would describe the minimum constitutional changes necessary to create a federal republic of Australia. The Committee consulted widely throughout Australia and talked to many different groups. As a result of the consultations, they delivered a report to the Government which was used to formulate the Government's position on the Australian republic. A period of active public discussion has been embarked upon to prepare for a referendum which the Government intends to hold.  THE REPUBLIC AND THE CONSTITUTION.  The Coalition's Position.  HEAD OF STATE.  • "The issue of Australia's Head of State will be debated first and separate from the other issues. Options for change will include electing the President by direct popular vote, as well as by a Parliamentary vote as proposed by the Prime Minister. The option of retaining the present system would be included in any vote," (Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The President would be appointed in a joint sitting of the Commonwealth Parliament, following the nomination of a single individual by the Prime Minister. The appointment has to be approved by a two-thirds majority of a joint sitting. This means that there will need to be prior bi-partisan agreement to the nominee.  Comment.  It is envisaged that the President would perform the ceremonial and representational functions currently performed by the monarch or the Governor-General. Election of the President by popular vote would create confusion about the respective roles of the President, the Parliament and the Government.  Attorney-General's. INTERNATIONAL LAW, EXTERNAL AFFAIRS POWER & TREATIES.  The Coalition's Position.  - "We will reform Australia's international treaty-making processes to ensure that the Australian Parliament, the States, industry and the community are consulted before they are entered into on Australia's behalf." (John Howard "The Austria I believe In', 15 December 1995).  - "We will ensure that there is a detailed public statement of the implications of international treaties on Australia's law, economy, environment and trade competitiveness before they are signed." (Liberall Party Speakers Notes, November 1995).  - "We will refer the question of the external affairs power to the People's Convention for consideration." (Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Government is committed to the proper level of involvement of Parliament, the States, industry and the community In treaty marten. It will continue to build upon recent improvements @ has made In the level of consultation with all those entities.  The Federal Labor Government will build upon the improvements which It has already made In the level and detail of the information being provided to all sectors on the implication of treaties, including an explanatory statement for each treaty. The Federal Labor Government supports the involvement of State, territory and local governments in treaty implementation. However, the external affairs power in its current form is necessary to ensure that all Australia is in a position to give effect to its international obligations. A change to that power is unnecessary and undesirable.  Comment.  In late November 1995 the Senate Legal & Constitutional Committee tabled its report into treaties, entitled Trick or Treaty. The Government is considering its response to the report.  Attorney-General's. INTERNATIONAL LAW. EXTERNAL AFFAIRS POWER & TREATIES.  The Coalition's Position.  THE JUSTICE STATEMENT.  • The Coalition has described The Justice Statement as disappointing. Senator Vanstone said that she expected a lot more. (Amanda Vanstone—press release - 18 May 1995).  LEGAL PROFESSION ETC.  • The Coalition described reforms of the legal  profession in New South Wales and South Australia as 'good examples'. (Amanda Vanstone—press release—18 May 1995).  DISCRIMINATION PROTECTIONS.  • John Howard has said that he believes that there should be "no discrimination on the grounds of religion, race, gender, ethnicity or nationality". (John Howard, "The Australia I Believe In', 15 December 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Justice Statement is one of the most comprehensive legal policy reforms ever presented in this country. The Coalition has provided no detail of its alternate policies. Senator Vanstone refused to disclose them on the basis that the Government might 'pinch them'. (Source: ABC Radio Interview—ZCN— Elizabeth Jackson—-19 May 1895). The fact that Howard left out disability shows his Jack of commitment to protecting all disadvantaged groups from discrimination. The Government is working with the States to create a National Legal Services Market. This will involve reform of the profession including the application of the national competition policy principles.  The Federal Labor Government has passed legislation which also makes discrimination unlawful on the ground of marital status and disability. People also have the right to make complaints to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission if they are discriminated against in employment on the additional grounds of age, political opinion, social origin, sexual preference, trade union activity, or medical or criminal record.  Comment.  The reforms proposed by the Coalition are not inconsistent with the Government's approach. In any event, the power to reform the legal profession reside overwhelmingly with the States and Territories.  Attorney-General's. LEGAL PROFESSION REFORM, HUMAN RIGHTS.  The Coalition's Position.  PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES. "There is an unacceptable backlog of disability discrimination cases." (Liberal Party Speakers Notes, November 1995).  WOMEN & EMPLOYMENT. The Coalition says that it will work to @@ all forms of discrimination against women" and "promote equality of opportunity for women" (Liberal Party Speakers /Votes, November 1995).  OLDER PEOPLE. The Coalition says it will "abolish age discrimination against the elderly". (Liberal Party Speakers Notes. November 1995).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government introduced the disability discrimination legislation and is committed to ensuring an efficient and effective mechanisms for resolving complaints. The Labor Government announced In 1994 a three stage program to reform and improve the Sex Discrimination Act to further protect and promote the position of women in the workplace. Stages one and two have now been enacted through reforms to the Act, and stage 3 will be delivered in 1996. The Federal Labor Government abolished compulsory age retirement in the Australian Public Service In 1995, and has a Task Force developing both legislative and non-legislative options to eliminate age discrimination in both the public and private sectors.  Comment.  Disability complaint handling at the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission is being reviewed and has improved significantly this year due to the work of a special task force to deal with complaints. The Coalition opposed some of Federal Labor's 1995 changes to the Sex Discrimination Act and Affirmative Action Act which aimed at making the process of proving sex discrimination cases fairer for women. They are more interested in keeping employers happy than in looking after the interests of women workers. The Coalition have not stated whether they will introduce Commonwealth age discrimination legislation or not. The Government also is not yet committed to the option of legislation.  Attorney-General's. JUSTICE.  The Coalition's Position.  CRIME.  The coalition says that in Government it would "ensure that the community has more protection from crime and violence." confidential Liberal "speakers notes' November 1995. The Coalition's Position.  -"We will reduce the unfair burden of the compliance cost of taxation through a range of specific tax reform initiatives.  - we will increase consultation prior to announcements of changes in tax policy and implement lime limits within which tax legislation is introduced following such announcements,  - we will simplify the concepts underlying tax law instead of merely re-drafling them in different language.  - we will include a Taxpayer's Charter of Rights in legislation and make it legally enforceable against the Tax Office " (John Howard, The Australia I Believe In). National Saving & Retirement Incomes Policies. SUPERANNUATION.  The Coalition's Position.  - Coalition will retain the Superannuation guarantee and proceed with the 3 per cent employee contribution (John Howard, The Australia I Believe In).  - Coalition will introduce "greater competition and choice in the management of superannuation", (John Howard, The Australia I Believe In).  - Coalition will "allow the introduction @ Savings Accounts by banks and other approved financial institutions" (John Howard, The Australia I Believe In).  LABOR'S POSITION.  The Federal Labor Government has revolutionised Australia's retirement incomes system. In 1983 fewer than 40 per cent of employees had superannuation, today that number is almost 90 per cent.  The Government requires superannuation trustees to seek the best returns for their members. In turn, this promotes vigorous competition between superannuation administrators and fund managers.  Government already allows Banks to offer superannuation through subsidiaries, which are subject to the same trustee obligations and regulations as all other superannuation funds.  Comment.  Open member choice would be an administrative nightmare for employers — an employer would have to make contributions to a multitude of funds according to the individual preferences of its employees. In building up Australia's superannuation system, the Government has been trying to build up a pool of long term investment funds, knowing that this is vital to securing Australia's economic future, as well as maximising retirement incomes. Under the Coalition's proposal to allow open member choice, super funds will have to be prepared to pay out funds to their members who could withdraw at any time. Long-term thinking will come to an end, reducing end benefits for members. Superannuation funds will have to keep liquid reserves — low return cash and securities, or even bank deposits. Short-term thinking, liquidity instead of growth, cash and deposits instead of equity and infrastructure will be the order of the day. The Coalition has not said whether banks will be obliged to have a trustee structure for their retirement savings accounts. The importance of the trustee arrangements for superannuation cannot be overstated. As well as providing a uniform basis for the prudential regulation of superannuation savings, the trustee arrangements ensure that the investment and management of those savings is undertaken exclusively for the benefit of superannuation fund members, A bank's primary responsibility, on the other hand, is to its shareholders.
